| OpenRouter (OpenAI-compatible adapter) | `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_KEY`; optional `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_BASE_URL` (default OpenRouter), `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_MODEL` (default `openai/gpt-6-luna`), `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_REASONING_EFFORT` (default `none`, empty omits it) |
| Anthropic | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`; optional `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` |
| Gemini | `GEMINI_API_KEY` (or `GOOGLE_API_KEY`); optional `GEMINI_MODEL` (default `gemini-3.1-flash-lite`). Free tier: about 5 requests a minute and 20 a day per model, so requests are spaced 13 s, a 429 skips the scenario with a message, and only S1 to S3 run by default |
| Ollama (OpenAI-compatible adapter, `Preset::Ollama`, no key) | `OLLAMA_MODEL` (required, one model per run; the test skips without it); optional `OLLAMA_BASE_URL` (default `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1`), `OLLAMA_REASONING_EFFORT` (default `none`, empty omits the field), `OLLAMA_MAX_TOKENS` (default 600), `OLLAMA_SCENARIOS`. The test is `live_ollama`; the latency test is `ollama_voice_latency` in `crates/brisvox-providers/tests/openai_compatible/live.rs` (`OLLAMA_RUNS`, default 5) |
| Gemini Live (S2S stage) | the Gemini key; optional `GEMINI_LIVE_MODEL` (default `gemini-3.8-live`); S1 and S2 only |

`BRISVOX_LIVE_SCENARIOS=1,2,6` picks scenarios for every provider; `OPENROUTER_SCENARIOS`,
`ANTHROPIC_SCENARIOS`, `GEMINI_SCENARIOS` and `GEMINI_LIVE_SCENARIOS` override per provider. A run
prints, per scenario, every round (time to first event and to first text, total, calls, text bytes),
every tool (start, finish, dropped), the runner's counters and what was spoken, then
`LIVE RESULT <provider> scenario <n>: ok|FAILED (<seconds> s)`. The live scenarios 5 and 6 use real
time (1 s tool, 0.4 s filler; 0.6 s booking). Gemini Live drives the engine's S2S stage with a
recorded sentence of the FLEURS fixtures ("The East African Islands are in the Indian Ocean off the
eastern coast of Africa."): the prompt turns it into three independent lookups (S1) or a
country -> capital -> weather chain (S2).

### Live results

Run 2026-10-14 (`BRISVOX_LIVE_TESTS=1 cargo test -p brisvox-engine --all-features --test
tool_scenarios live_ -- --nocapture --test-threads=1`; Gemini text requests spaced 13 s for the
free tier). Cells: result, the issuing round's time to first event, rounds.

| Scenario | OpenRouter `openai/gpt-6-luna` | Anthropic (Haiku 5.5) | Gemini `gemini-3.1-flash-lite` | Gemini Live `gemini-3.8-live` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 parallel (3 calls in one response) | ok: 3 calls, TTFT 2.0 s, 1 tool round, total 4.0 s | ok: 3 calls, 1.4 s, 1 round, 3.3 s | ok: 3 calls, 1.8 s, 1 round | ok: 3 calls run together (307 ms phase), spoken answer |
| S2 chain (3 rounds) | ok: 3 rounds, 1.1-1.2 s per round, 6.1 s | ok: 3 rounds, 0.6-1.1 s per round, 5.1 s | ok: 3 rounds (spaced 13 s) | ok: Africa -> Algeria -> Algiers -> weather, 3 rounds |
| S3 booking repeated | ok: booked once | ok: booked once | ok | n/a |
| S4 invalid args | ok: retried with valid args | ok | n/a | n/a |
| S5 slow tool + filler | ok: 1 filler | ok: 1 filler | n/a | n/a |
| S6 barge-in | ok: late note next turn | ok: late note next turn | n/a | n/a |

Gemini Live first failed every connect: the adapter sent the raw JSON Schema in `parameters`,
which takes only Gemini's OpenAPI subset and refuses the setup on `additionalProperties`; it now
sends `parametersJsonSchema` (fixed with this run).

### Local models through Ollama

Run 2026-10-14 against Ollama 0.34.1 on Windows, an RTX 5070 (12 GB), through the same engine path
as the table above (`LlmRunner` + `ToolEngine`, the OpenAI-compatible adapter with
`preset = "ollama"`, `reasoning_effort = "none"`, sampling left at each model's Ollama defaults, the
server's default context of 4096 tokens). One model at a time:

```text
OLLAMA_MODEL=gemma4:12b-it-qat BRISVOX_LIVE_TESTS=1 cargo test -p brisvox-engine --all-features   --test tool_scenarios live_ollama -- --nocapture --test-threads=1
OLLAMA_MODEL=gemma4:12b-it-qat BRISVOX_LIVE_TESTS=1 cargo test -p brisvox-providers --all-features   --test openai_compatible ollama_voice_latency -- --nocapture
```

Each model ran the six scenarios three times (18 runs). Latency: a one-to-two sentence voice
prompt on a warm model, five runs, p50 of the time to the first text token and to the end of the
first sentence. The GPU had room for every model (no other large GPU process was resident), so
"GPU memory" is the full footprint that `/api/ps` reports at the 4096 context.

| Model | Params, quant | GPU memory | Scenarios passed (of 18) | TTFT p50 | First sentence p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `gemma4:12b-it-qat` | 11.9B, Q4_0 | 7.7 GB (all on GPU) | **18/18**: S1 to S6 each 3/3 | 69 ms | 267 ms |
| `gemma4:e4b-it-qat` | 7.5B (4B effective), Q4_0 | 3.1 GB | 12/18: S2 0/3, S4 0/3, rest 3/3 | 42 ms | 157 ms |
| `qwen3.5:4b` | 4.7B, Q4_K_M | 3.1 GB | 12/18: S2 0/3, S4 0/3, rest 3/3 | 65 ms | 208 ms |
| `qwen3.5:9b` | 9.7B, Q4_K_M | 5.5 GB | 12/18: S1 2/3, S2 2/3, S4 0/3, S5 2/3, S3 and S6 3/3 | 79 ms | 291 ms |
| `qwen2.5-coder:7b` | 7.6B, Q4_K_M | 4.7 GB | 0/18 | 34 ms | 220 ms |

How the others fail (the failures are the models', not the engine's; the engine refused every bad
call and ran every good one):

- **S2, a chain whose second call needs the first result.** `qwen3.5:4b` and, once in three,
  `qwen3.5:9b` call `get_customer` and `get_weather` in the same response with a guessed city
  (Rome, Paris) instead of waiting for `get_customer`. `gemma4:e4b-it-qat` answered nothing at all
  (an empty response, no text and no call).
- **S4, an invalid argument (`days` above its maximum).** Every model but `gemma4:12b-it-qat` read
  the structured `invalid_arguments` result, said "I will ask for three days instead" and ended the
  turn without calling the tool again. The caller hears a promise that is never kept.
- **S1 and S5.** `qwen3.5:9b` once answered the three-city question and once the slow Izmir
  question with made-up weather, without calling any tool (a hallucinated answer, the worst
  failure for a voice agent).
- **`qwen2.5-coder:7b`** never emits a native tool call: it writes the call as JSON text
  (`{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": ...}`), which the agent would speak aloud. S6 also waited
  its full 120 s for tools that never started. Do not use it for tools.

Thinking. `qwen3.5` and `gemma4` are thinking models that think by default on Ollama.
`reasoning_effort = "none"` on the OpenAI-compatible endpoint turns that off and is what the table
used (a model without a thinking mode, `qwen2.5-coder`, accepts the field). The native field
`think: false` is ignored on `/v1/chat/completions` (`qwen3.5:4b` spent 300 of 300 tokens on
reasoning and returned an empty answer). Without the setting, `qwen3.5:4b` produced no spoken text
inside a 200-token budget. With `reasoning_effort = "medium"`, `qwen3.5:9b` passed 12/12 scenario
runs, but the plain chat prompts took 14 to 35 s to the first spoken word (TTFT p50 22 s), and
`qwen3.5:4b` still failed S2: thinking buys tool reliability at a price a call cannot pay.

Partial offload. `gemma4:12b-it-qat` needs 7.7 GB. With only 5 GB of GPU memory free (the Kokoro
voice server resident next to it), 30 of its 48 layers on the GPU (4.96 GB) gave TTFT p50 376 ms
and first sentence p50 1.66 s on the same prompts (measured through Ollama's native
`/api/chat` with `num_gpu = 30` and `think = false`, because `/v1` has no per-request options;
the model is the same, the adapter adds a few ms). That is usable for a call but no longer
fast: either give the language model the GPU alone (Kokoro's CPU image), or accept the 1.7 s.
The first request after a model was idle paid its load: 7 to 50 s (cold) in these runs, so warm
the model before a call (`OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1` keeps it resident).

Recommendation: `gemma4:12b-it-qat` for any agent with tools, `reasoning_effort = "none"` always.
Without tools, `gemma4:e4b-it-qat` is the fastest (157 ms to the first sentence in 3.1 GB). The
example agents in `examples/agents/local/` use the first. Three runs per model is a small sample:
a model that passed 3/3 here can still fail on a prompt the scenarios do not cover, so try your own
tools.


<!-- source: sdk/python/README.md -->

# brisvox-agent (Python SDK)

The agent side of the brisvox agent protocol (`docs/AGENT_PROTOCOL.md`, version 1): write the
application logic of a real-time voice call in async Python. The brisvox server connects **out**
to your agent over a WebSocket, one connection per call; this package is the WebSocket server
and the typed API on top of it.

Python 3.11 or newer, one dependency (`websockets`, `>=15,<16`: the range the suite is run on, 15.0.1).

```python
from brisvox_agent import Agent, Session, UserText

agent = Agent("luigi", system_prompt="You are Luigi's host.", greeting="Hi, Luigi's here!")

@agent.tool                                   # JSON schema from the type hints
async def opening_hours(day: str) -> str:
    """Opening hours of the restaurant on a weekday."""
    return "12:00 to 22:00"

@agent.on_user_text
async def heard(session: Session, event: UserText) -> None:
    if "bye" in event.text.lower():
        await session.end("Goodbye!")         # speaks the farewell, then ends the call

agent.run(port=8765)                          # then: BRISVOX_AGENT_URL=ws://127.0.0.1:8765
```

Install from PyPI: `pip install brisvox-agent` (`pip install brisvox` installs the same SDK under the short name; `import brisvox` is `import brisvox_agent`). From a checkout of the repository: `pip install ./sdk/python`
(or `pip install -e './sdk/python[test]'`).

**Where it listens.** `host` defaults to `127.0.0.1`: only a server on the same machine can reach
the agent. For a brisvox server in another container or service bind `0.0.0.0` (IPv4) or `::`
(IPv6; `::` on a private network that may be IPv6-only, such as Railway's), set `BRISVOX_AGENT_TOKEN`, and give the server the
agent's name in `BRISVOX_AGENT_URL`. `agent.run()` logs the address it bound at INFO, or prints
it to stderr when logging is not configured, and on a loopback address the line says so:
`agent 'luigi' listening on ws://127.0.0.1:8765 (loopback: reachable only from this machine; bind 0.0.0.0 or :: for a server in another container)`.

## What you get

| Protocol | SDK |
|---|---|
| Handshake, version negotiation | Automatic. The highest version both sides speak is picked; none in common sends `session.reject` with `unsupported_version`. `@agent.on_session_start` may return `Accept(...)` (prompt, context, greeting, events, tools for this call) or raise `Reject(code, message)`. |
| `session.accept` fields | `Agent(system_prompt=, context=, greeting=, events=)`. `events="auto"` (default) subscribes only to the event types you registered handlers for. |
| Events | `@agent.on_user_text`, `on_transcript`, `on_bot_text`, `on_turn`, `on_error`, `on_events_lost`, `on_resumed`, `on_session_end`, or any event by class: `@agent.on(TurnInterrupted)` / `@agent.on("bot.tts_text")`. Typed frozen dataclasses (`brisvox_agent.protocol`). Handlers of one call run one at a time, in order. |
| Remote tools | `@agent.tool(kind="read_only" or "side_effect", timeout_ms=, filler_after_ms=)`. Schema from type hints (`str int float bool list dict Optional Literal Enum dataclass date datetime Annotated[T, "doc"]`) and the docstring (`Args:`). Arguments arrive converted to the hinted types. Add `ctx: ToolContext` for the `idempotency_key`, `epoch`, and the cancel signal. Plain `def` tools run on a worker thread. |
| `tool.cancel` | `read_only`: the tool task is cancelled (`asyncio.CancelledError`). `side_effect`: not cancelled (advice only), `ctx.cancelled` is set; the result still goes out and becomes a late note. |
| Commands | `await session.say(text, interrupt=)`, `end(say=, reason=)`, `transfer(destination, mode=, summary=, reason=, id=)`, `update_context(system_prompt=, append=)`, `set_tools(names or None)`. Each awaits its `command.result` and raises `CommandError(code)` (an `ErrorCode`) on refusal; `wait=False` returns a future instead. |
| `re` | Taken from the event the handler is reacting to, so the server can measure the hop latency. Pass `re=` to override. |
| Rules of the doc | Checked before sending (4 KiB lines, E.164 numbers, 512-byte notes, 32 messages, 64 KiB messages, id <= 64 bytes): a violation raises `CommandError(invalid_argument / too_large)` locally. |
| Auth | `agent.serve(token=...)` / `BRISVOX_AGENT_TOKEN`: the `Authorization: Bearer` header is checked in constant time, else HTTP 401. |

## Things to know

* **Bind address.** `run()` and `serve()` listen on `127.0.0.1` by default, which only a brisvox
  server on the same machine can reach. When the server runs in another container or service
  (Docker Compose, Kubernetes, a PaaS), bind all interfaces: `agent.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=8765)`
  (`host="::"` where the private network can be IPv6-only, as on Railway; dual-stack on Linux), and set
  `BRISVOX_AGENT_TOKEN` on both sides. An agent the server cannot reach is not an error for the
  call: it runs on the agent file alone, without your tools. `docs/DEPLOY.md`, "Your tools service".

* **In a container.** `pip install brisvox-agent` in the image is enough. The template in this
  repository vendors the SDK instead: the build context is a checkout of this repository and
  `pip install` runs on the copied `sdk/python`.
  `examples/booking-agent/Dockerfile` is the template
  (`docker build -f examples/booking-agent/Dockerfile -t booking-agent .` from the repository
  root); it binds all interfaces and runs as a non-root user. `docs/DEPLOY.md`, "Your tools service".

* **Errors in tools.** `raise ToolError("no tables left")` tells the LLM exactly that message.
  Any other exception tells the LLM only `tool failed: <ExceptionType>`; the details stay in your
  log, never on the phone line.
* **Transfers.** Give a transfer an `id` you can reproduce (`id=f"handoff-{session.id}"`).
  After a `CommandTimeout` (the outcome is unknown) repeat it **with the same id** and the carrier
  deduplicates; a transfer without an id is a new transfer every time (the SDK generates a fresh id
  when you pass none). `session.capabilities.transfer` tells whether the server can transfer.
* **Confirmation gate.** `@agent.tool(kind="side_effect", confirm=True)` holds the tool for the
  user's confirmation: the model's call does not run it, the model gets a `confirmation_required`
  result, asks the user, and the tool runs only when the model calls the built-in `confirm_pending`
  after the user's NEXT reply (`docs/TOOLS.md`, "Confirmation gate"). A barge-in cancels the held
  request. `confirm` needs a `side_effect` tool (`ValueError` on a read-only one); the name
  `confirm_pending` is reserved. Your handler runs once, with the original arguments, when confirmed.
* **Who is calling.** `session.call` is `None` unless the agent definition opted in
  (`[agent_link] caller_identity = true`, or `BRISVOX_AGENT_CALLER_IDENTITY=1`) and the call comes
  through a carrier (Twilio, Telnyx, SIP). Then it is a `CallIdentity` with `carrier`,
  `carrier_call_id` (Twilio `CallSid`, Telnyx `call_control_id`, SIP `Call-ID`), `from_number`,
  `to_number` and `pii_redacted` (the wire fields are `from` and `to`; the TypeScript SDK names
  them `from` and `to` too). The numbers are `None` when the carrier did not say or when
  the server redacts phone numbers (`docs/PRIVACY.md`); with Twilio they exist only when the
  TwiML passes them as stream parameters `from` and `to` (`docs/TELEPHONY.md`). A caller ID can
  be spoofed: use it as a hint, and keep it out of your logs (`repr()` of a `CallIdentity` omits
  the numbers). A malformed `call` object is ignored (`session.call` stays `None`).
* **Repeating a side effect.** The server refuses an identical `side_effect` call (same
  arguments) that the model repeats in a later response of the same turn, answering
  `already_done` without calling your handler: a second booking is almost never wanted.
  `@agent.tool(kind="side_effect", repeatable=True)` lets such a repeat through, for a tool where
  doing the same thing twice is legitimate (pressing the same IVR digit twice). `repeatable`
  needs a `side_effect` tool (`ValueError` on a read-only one, like `confirm`).
* **Slow handlers** never delay tool results or command results (they are handled on the reader),
  but they delay later events of the same call. The per-call handler queue is bounded
  (`Agent(event_queue=1024)`); when it overflows the newest events are dropped and the handlers
  get an `EventsLost` in front of the next event after the gap, exactly like the server's own
  backpressure policy. `session.end` is never dropped.
* **Session end.** `on_session_end` runs once per call; if the link dropped without
  `session.end` the reason is `"link_closed"`. When the link drops every running tool sees `ctx.cancelled` (reason
  `"link_closed"`); `read_only` tools are cancelled, `side_effect` tools get
  `Agent(side_effect_grace=30)` seconds to wind down before they are cancelled.
* **Limits.** `Agent(max_sessions=256)`; more calls are answered with `session.reject`
  (`unavailable`). The handshake handler must finish inside `handshake_timeout` (1.5 s; the server
  gives up at 2 s).

## Reconnecting (`resume`)

By default a lost link ends the call for the handlers (`on_session_end`, reason `"link_closed"`),
and the server does not reopen it. Opt in with `Agent(resume=True)` when the agent can keep a
call's state across a dropped connection (the protocol's "Reconnecting", `docs/AGENT_PROTOCOL.md`):

```python
agent = Agent("luigi", resume=True, resume_window=15.0)

@agent.on_session_start
async def started(session):           # once per call, never for a resumption
    session.data["notes"] = []

@agent.on_resumed
async def back(session, event):       # attempt, previous_seq, down_ms
    log.info("link back after %d ms", event.down_ms)
```

* `session.accept` then carries `"resume": true`. When the link is lost the `Session` is *parked*:
  `session.data`, the queued events and the handlers' view of the call stay. Commands raise
  `SessionClosed` meanwhile (`session.parked` is true, `session.closed` too); commands waiting for a
  result fail at the loss, and running tools see `ctx.cancelled` (reason `"link_closed"`) as
  usual. A `side_effect` call that was in flight has an unknown outcome on the server's side and is
  never repeated.
* The server's next `session.start` carries `resume` (`attempt`, `previous_seq`, `down_ms`; its `seq`
  continues the call's count). The SDK answers `session.accept` with `resume: true` and the same
  event subscription, re-attaches the parked session to the new link and runs `on_resumed` after
  the events queued before the loss. There is no greeting and no `on_session_start`;
  `tools`, `system_prompt` and `context` are ignored by the server on a resumption, so the first
  declaration stands. `session.resumes` counts the resumptions of the call.
* What the server could not deliver meanwhile is not replayed: it reports the number as
  `events.lost` (so `on_events_lost` runs). An agent that needs the conversation reads it from its
  own store or asks for it with `update_context`.
* If the server does not come back within `resume_window` seconds (default 15, the server's own
  reconnect window) the call ends for the handlers once (`on_session_end`, `"link_closed"`) and the
  parked state is dropped; a later resumption is answered with `session.reject` `unknown_session`.
  A `session.end` from the server is final at once. Stopping the server (`AgentServer.close`)
  ends parked calls immediately.
* A resumption that arrives while the old link still looks open (half-open TCP) takes the session
  over and closes the old link.
* The state lives in this process. An agent that restarts has nothing to resume: it answers with
  `unknown_session` and the server goes on without it. Keep the state in a shared store if it must
  outlive the process (and route a resumption to the process that holds the call).

## Session tokens for browsers

The server's browser-facing listeners (WebRTC, RTVI, generic WebSocket) accept short-lived,
single-use tokens your backend signs with `BRISVOX_SESSION_SECRET` (`docs/SECURITY.md`):

```python
from brisvox_agent.session_token import mint_session_token

token = mint_session_token(os.environ["BRISVOX_SESSION_SECRET"], "brisvox-webrtc",
                           ttl=60, agent="support", max_s=600, meta={"user": "u-42"})
```

`ttl`, `max_s` and `now` are whole **seconds**: `ttl` is 1 to 86400 (the server refuses a token that
lives longer than 24 hours, which would also fill its single-use set), `max_s` 1 to 86400, and a `now`
that looks like milliseconds raises `ValueError`.

## Examples

* `examples/minimal.py`: the Python twin of the minimal agent in the protocol doc.
* `examples/restaurant.py`: typed tools (enum, nested dataclass, `side_effect` with an
  idempotency key), per-call setup, and every command.
* `examples/resumable.py`: `resume=True`, `on_resumed`, per-call state that survives a dropped
  link.

## Tests

```
python -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e '.[test]'
.venv/bin/python -m pytest
```

* `tests/test_protocol.py`: message (de)serialization against the examples and tables of
  `docs/AGENT_PROTOCOL.md` (it reads the doc: error codes, event names and limits must match).
* `tests/test_tools.py`: schema generation and argument conversion.
* `tests/test_agent.py`, `tests/test_examples.py`: the agent over a real WebSocket against a fake
  brisvox server (`tests/fake_server.py`) that replays the doc's sequences.
* `tests/test_resume.py`: reconnecting (parking, resumption, expiry, takeover of a half-open link).
* **Against the real Rust link:** `crates/brisvox-agent-link/tests/python_sdk.rs` runs a call
  (loopback transport, mock providers) linked to `examples/restaurant.py` in a Python process:
  greeting, a `side_effect` and a `read_only` tool, and an agent-initiated `end`. It runs when
  `BRISVOX_PYTHON_SDK` names a Python (3.11+) that has `websockets`. `scripts/verify.sh` finds one,
  runs the whole Python suite (`python -m unittest discover -s tests -t tests` in `sdk/python`)
  and sets the variable for the Rust test. A second test of the file cuts the link of a call in
  the middle (a TCP proxy drops the sockets) and checks that `examples/resumable.py` takes the
  call up again: state kept, `seq` continuing, tools still working. CI sets
  `BRISVOX_REQUIRE_PYTHON_SDK=1`, so there a missing Python fails the gate instead of skipping it:

  ```
  BRISVOX_PYTHON_SDK=.venv/bin/python cargo nextest run -p brisvox-agent-link --test python_sdk
  ```


<!-- source: sdk/typescript/README.md -->

# @brisvox/agent (TypeScript SDK)

The agent side of the brisvox agent protocol (`docs/AGENT_PROTOCOL.md`, version 1): write the
application logic of a real-time voice call in async TypeScript. The brisvox server connects **out**
to your agent over a WebSocket, one connection per call; this package is the WebSocket server and
the typed API on top of it. It mirrors the Python SDK (`sdk/python`) one to one.

Node 20 or newer, ESM, TypeScript `strict`. One runtime dependency: `ws` (pinned to 8.22.0, the
version the suite runs on). No schema library: tool parameters use a small builder in `src/schema.ts` (see "Tools").

```ts
import { Agent, s } from "@brisvox/agent";

const agent = new Agent({ name: "luigi", systemPrompt: "You are Luigi's host.", greeting: "Hi, Luigi's here!" });

agent.tool({
  name: "opening_hours",
  description: "Opening hours of the restaurant on a weekday.",
  parameters: s.object({ day: s.enum(["mon", "tue", "wed", "thu", "fri", "sat", "sun"]) }),
  handler: async ({ day }) => (day === "mon" ? "Closed on Monday." : "12:00 to 22:00."), // day is typed
});

agent.onUserText(async (session, event) => {
  if (event.text.toLowerCase().includes("bye")) {
    await session.end({ say: "Goodbye!" }); // speaks the farewell, then ends the call
  }
});

await agent.run({ port: 8765 }); // then: BRISVOX_AGENT_URL=ws://127.0.0.1:8765
```

Install from npm: `npm install @brisvox/agent` (`npm i brisvox` re-exports it under the short name: `import { Agent } from "brisvox"`). From a checkout of the repository:
`npm install ./sdk/typescript` after `npm run build` in it, or work in the repository directly.

**Where it listens.** `host` defaults to `127.0.0.1`: only a server on the same machine can reach
the agent. For a brisvox server in another container or service bind `0.0.0.0` (IPv4) or `::`
(IPv6; `::` on a private network that may be IPv6-only, such as Railway's), set `BRISVOX_AGENT_TOKEN`, and give the server the
agent's name in `BRISVOX_AGENT_URL`. `agent.run()` logs the address it bound at `info` (printed
to stderr when the default logger, which shows warnings only, would drop it), and on a loopback
address the line says so:
`agent 'luigi' listening on ws://127.0.0.1:8765 (loopback: reachable only from this machine; bind 0.0.0.0 or :: for a server in another container)`.

## What you get

| Protocol | SDK |
|---|---|
| Handshake, version negotiation | Automatic. The highest version both sides speak is picked; none in common sends `session.reject` with `unsupported_version`. `agent.onSessionStart(...)` may return `{ systemPrompt, context, greeting, events, tools }` for this call or throw `new Reject(code, message)`. |
| `session.accept` fields | `new Agent({ systemPrompt, context, greeting, events })`. `events: "auto"` (default) subscribes only to the event types you registered handlers for. |
| Events | `agent.onUserText`, `onTranscript`, `onBotText`, `onTurn`, `onError`, `onEventsLost`, `onResumed`, `onSessionEnd`, or any event by wire type: `agent.on("turn.interrupted", ...)`. Events are readonly objects with a `type` discriminant (so `if (event.type === "turn.metrics")` narrows), camelCase fields (`tMs`, `sessionId`). Handlers of one call run one at a time, in order. |
| Remote tools | `agent.tool({ name, description, parameters, handler, kind, timeoutMs, fillerAfterMs, confirm, repeatable })`. With `parameters: s.object({...})` the handler's `args` are typed and validated; with a plain JSON-schema object they arrive as sent. The handler's second argument is a `ToolContext` (`idempotencyKey`, `epoch`, `signal`, `session`). |
| Who is calling | `session.call` is `undefined` unless the agent definition opted in (`[agent_link] caller_identity = true`, or `BRISVOX_AGENT_CALLER_IDENTITY=1`) and the call comes through a carrier (Twilio, Telnyx, SIP). Then it is a `CallIdentity`: `carrier`, `carrierCallId` (Twilio `CallSid`, Telnyx `call_control_id`, SIP `Call-ID`), `from`, `to` and `piiRedacted` (the Python SDK calls `from` and `to` `from_number` and `to_number`). The numbers are absent when the carrier did not say or when the server redacts phone numbers (`docs/PRIVACY.md`); with Twilio they exist only when the TwiML passes them as stream parameters `from` and `to` (`docs/TELEPHONY.md`). A caller ID can be spoofed: use it as a hint, and keep it out of your logs. |
| Repeating a side effect | The server refuses an identical `side_effect` call (same arguments) that the model repeats in a later response of the same turn, answering `already_done` without calling your handler. `repeatable: true` lets such a repeat through, for a tool where doing the same thing twice is legitimate (pressing the same IVR digit twice). It needs `kind: "side_effect"` (`RangeError` on a read-only tool, like `confirm`). |
| `tool.cancel` | `read_only`: `ctx.signal` aborts and the SDK stops waiting (no result is sent). `side_effect`: `ctx.signal` aborts as advice, the tool is not stopped, its result still goes out and becomes a late note. |
| Commands | `await session.say(text, { interrupt })`, `end({ say, reason })`, `transfer(destination, { mode, summary, reason, id })`, `updateContext({ systemPrompt, append })`, `setTools(names \| null)`. Each awaits its `command.result` and throws `CommandError` (`.code` is an `ErrorCode`) on refusal; `{ wait: false }` returns `{ id, result: Promise }` instead. |
| `re` | Taken from the event the handler is reacting to (an `AsyncLocalStorage`), so the server can measure the hop latency. Pass `{ re: 12 }` to override, `{ re: null }` to send none. |
| Rules of the doc | Checked before sending (4 KiB lines, E.164 numbers, 512-byte notes, 32 messages, 64 KiB messages, id <= 64 bytes): a violation throws `CommandError(invalid_argument / too_large)` locally. |
| Auth | `agent.listen({ token })` / `BRISVOX_AGENT_TOKEN`: the `Authorization: Bearer` header is checked in constant time, else HTTP 401 before any frame. `tls: { key, cert }` serves `wss://`. |

## Tools

```ts
const params = s.object({
  time: s.string({ description: "HH:MM, 24 hours" }),
  party_size: s.optional(s.integer({ minimum: 1, maximum: 12 }), 2),   // default 2: always a number in the handler
  contact: s.optional(s.object({ name: s.string(), phone: s.optional(s.string()) })),
});
```

`s.string / number / integer / boolean / enum / array / object / nullable / optional` build the JSON
Schema that goes into `session.accept` (property names are the names the LLM sees, so use the
snake_case you want it to use), validate the `arguments` of each call (a violation is answered to
the LLM as `invalid arguments: $.contact.name: is required`) and type the handler (`Infer<typeof
params>`). Extra properties are dropped. For anything the builder cannot say, pass a hand-written
JSON-schema object as `parameters`: the server validates those, and `args` is
`Record<string, unknown>`.

**Why not zod.** A tool schema needs a handful of node kinds. zod 4 (4.6.7 on npm today) is a large
dependency whose JSON-Schema export would be a second API to pin and keep in step with the server's
validator; the builder is dependency free, emits exactly the keywords the server compiles, and is
typed by inference. A zod user can pass `z.toJSONSchema(schema)` as a raw `parameters` object.

## Things to know

* **Bind address.** `run()` and `listen()` listen on `127.0.0.1` by default, which only a brisvox
  server on the same machine can reach. When the server runs in another container or service
  (Docker Compose, Kubernetes, a PaaS), bind all interfaces: `agent.run({ host: "0.0.0.0", port: 8765 })`
  (`host: "::"` where the private network can be IPv6-only, as on Railway; dual-stack on Linux), and set
  `BRISVOX_AGENT_TOKEN` on both sides. An agent the server cannot reach is not an error for the
  call: it runs on the agent file alone, without your tools. `docs/DEPLOY.md`, "Your tools service".

* **In a container.** `npm install @brisvox/agent` in the image is enough. The template in this
  repository builds the SDK instead: the build context is a
  checkout of this repository, `npm ci && npm run build` runs on the copied `sdk/typescript`, and
  `dist` plus the production `node_modules` go into the final stage.
  `sdk/typescript/examples/Dockerfile` is the template
  (`docker build -f sdk/typescript/examples/Dockerfile -t restaurant-agent .` from the repository
  root); it binds all interfaces and runs as a non-root user. Its header says how to vendor the
  build into your own package. `docs/DEPLOY.md`, "Your tools service".

* **Errors in tools.** `throw new ToolError("no tables left")` tells the LLM exactly that message.
  Any other error tells the LLM only `tool failed: <ClassName>`; the details stay in your log, never
  on the phone line. A result that is not strict JSON (NaN, Infinity, a cycle, a BigInt) or larger than
  64 KiB is answered with an error instead of hanging the call; `undefined` is sent as `null`.
* **Blocking work.** Handlers run on the event loop. A synchronous CPU-heavy tool stalls every call of
  the process (and its keep-alive): move that work to a `worker_threads` worker.
* **Cancellation is cooperative.** JavaScript cannot stop a running promise. The SDK stops *waiting*
  for a cancelled `read_only` tool and for a `side_effect` tool that outlives the link by
  `sideEffectGraceMs` (default 30 s); watch `ctx.signal` to actually stop the work.
* **Transfers.** Give a transfer an `id` you can reproduce (`id: \`handoff-${session.id}\``). After a
  `CommandTimeout` (the outcome is unknown) repeat it **with the same id** and the carrier
  deduplicates; a transfer without an id is a new transfer every time (the SDK generates a fresh id
  when you pass none). `session.capabilities.transfer` tells whether the server can transfer.
* **Slow handlers** never delay tool results or command results (they are handled on the reader),
  but they delay later events of the same call. The per-call handler queue is bounded
  (`eventQueue: 1024`); when it overflows the newest events are dropped and the handlers get an
  `events.lost` in front of the next event after the gap, exactly like the server's own backpressure
  policy. `session.end` is never dropped.
* **Session end.** `onSessionEnd` runs once per call; if the link dropped without `session.end` the
  reason is `"link_closed"`. When the link drops every running tool sees `ctx.signal` abort (reason
  `"link_closed"`); `read_only` tools are abandoned, `side_effect` tools get `sideEffectGraceMs` to wind
  down before the SDK stops waiting.
* **Limits.** `maxSessions: 256` (more calls are answered with `session.reject` `unavailable`),
  `maxConcurrentTools: 64` per call, incoming frames at most 128 KiB, `commandTimeoutMs: 10000`,
  `writeTimeoutMs: 10000` (a write that does not finish takes the link down). The handshake handler
  must finish inside `handshakeTimeoutMs` (1.5 s; the server gives up at 2 s).
* **Logs.** Warnings and errors go to `console.error`; `BRISVOX_AGENT_LOG=debug|info|warn|error|silent`
  or `new Agent({ logger })` changes that.

## Reconnecting (`resume`)

By default a lost link ends the call for the handlers (`onSessionEnd`, reason `"link_closed"`), and
the server does not reopen it. Opt in with `new Agent({ resume: true })` when the agent can keep a
call's state across a dropped connection (the protocol's "Reconnecting", `docs/AGENT_PROTOCOL.md`):

```ts
const agent = new Agent({ resume: true, resumeWindowMs: 15_000 });

agent.onSessionStart((session) => {   // once per call, never for a resumption
  session.data["notes"] = [];
});

agent.onResumed((session, event) => { // attempt, previousSeq, downMs
  console.error(`link back after ${event.downMs} ms`);
});
```

- `session.accept` then carries `"resume": true`. When the link is lost the `Session` is *parked*:
  `session.data`, the queued events and the handlers' view of the call stay. Commands reject with
  `SessionClosed` meanwhile (`session.parked` and `session.closed` are true); commands waiting for a
  result fail at the loss, and running tools see `ctx.signal` abort (reason `"link_closed"`) as
  usual. A `side_effect` call that was in flight has an unknown outcome on the server's side and is
  never repeated.
- The server's next `session.start` carries `resume` (`attempt`, `previous_seq`, `down_ms`; its `seq`
  continues the call's count). The SDK answers `session.accept` with `resume: true` and the same
  event subscription, re-attaches the parked session to the new link and runs `onResumed` after the
  events queued before the loss. There is no greeting and no `onSessionStart`; `tools`,
  `system_prompt` and `context` are ignored by the server on a resumption, so the first declaration
  stands. `session.resumes` counts the resumptions of the call.
- What the server could not deliver meanwhile is not replayed: it reports the number as
  `events.lost` (so `onEventsLost` runs). An agent that needs the conversation reads it from its own
  store or asks for it with `updateContext`.
- If the server does not come back within `resumeWindowMs` (default 15000, the server's own
  reconnect window) the call ends for the handlers once (`onSessionEnd`, `"link_closed"`) and the
  parked state is dropped; a later resumption is answered with `session.reject` `unknown_session`.
  A `session.end` from the server is final at once. Closing the server (`AgentServer.close`) ends
  parked calls immediately.
- A resumption that arrives while the old link still looks open (half-open TCP) takes the session
  over and closes the old link.
- The state lives in this process. An agent that restarts has nothing to resume: it answers with
  `unknown_session` and the server goes on without it. Keep the state in a shared store if it must
  outlive the process (and route a resumption to the process that holds the call).

## Session tokens for browsers

The server's browser-facing listeners (WebRTC, RTVI, generic WebSocket) accept short-lived,
single-use tokens your backend signs with `BRISVOX_SESSION_SECRET` (`docs/SECURITY.md`):

```ts
import { mintSessionToken } from "@brisvox/agent";

const token = mintSessionToken(process.env.BRISVOX_SESSION_SECRET!, "brisvox-webrtc", {
  ttlSeconds: 60,
  agent: "support",
  maxSeconds: 600,
  meta: { user: "u-42" },
});
```

## Examples

* `examples/minimal.ts`: the TypeScript twin of the minimal agent in the protocol doc.
* `examples/restaurant.ts`: typed tools (enum, nested object, `side_effect` with an idempotency
  key), per-call setup, and every command. It is also what `ts_sdk.rs` runs.
* `examples/resumable.ts`: `resume: true`, `onResumed`, per-call state that survives a dropped
  link.

Build and run (the examples import `../src/index.js`; in an application import `@brisvox/agent`):

```
npm ci && npm run build
node dist/examples/restaurant.js --port 8765
```

## Tests

```
npm ci
npm test            # tsc, then node:test over dist/tests (node:test: no test framework dependency)
```

* `tests/protocol.test.ts`: message (de)serialization against the examples and tables of
  `docs/AGENT_PROTOCOL.md` (it reads the doc: error codes, event names, limits and the two JSON
  examples must match).
* `tests/tools.test.ts`: schema generation, argument validation, inferred types (a compile-time check).
* `tests/resume.test.ts`: reconnecting (parking, resumption, expiry, takeover of a half-open link).
* `tests/handshake.test.ts`, `events.test.ts`, `tools-wire.test.ts`, `examples.test.ts`: the agent over
  a real WebSocket against a fake brisvox server (`tests/fake-server.ts`) that replays the doc's
  sequences.
* **Against the real Rust link:** `crates/brisvox-agent-link/tests/ts_sdk.rs` runs a call (loopback
  transport, mock providers) linked to `dist/examples/restaurant.js` in a Node process: greeting, a
  `side_effect` and a `read_only` tool, and an agent-initiated `end`, the same script as
  `python_sdk.rs`. It runs when `BRISVOX_TS_SDK` names a Node 20+ executable and the SDK is built.
  A second test of the file cuts the link of a call in the middle (a TCP proxy drops the sockets)
  and checks that `dist/examples/resumable.js` takes the call up again: state kept, `seq`
  continuing, tools still working.
  `scripts/verify.sh` installs (`npm ci`), builds, runs the whole suite and sets the variable; CI sets
  `BRISVOX_REQUIRE_TS_SDK=1`, so there a missing Node fails the gate instead of skipping it:

  ```
  BRISVOX_TS_SDK=node cargo nextest run -p brisvox-agent-link --test ts_sdk
  ```


<!-- source: examples/rust-tools/README.md -->

# Rust tools in your own server binary

A voice agent whose tools are written in Rust and run inside the server process. Use this shape
when your application logic is Rust and you want one binary; use the
[booking agent](../booking-agent) (Python SDK) when it lives in another process or language.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `src/main.rs` | The whole binary: `brisvox::run_with_tools(Arc::new(MyTools::default()))`. |
| `src/lib.rs` | `MyTools`, an `AppTools` implementation: a read-only `get_time(timezone)` and a side-effect `save_note(text)`, with tests. |
| `agent.toml` | The agent: Deepgram + OpenAI + Cartesia, and `tools = ["get_time", "save_note"]`. |
| `Cargo.toml` | Depends on `brisvox` (the umbrella crate: server, tools API, core types) with the provider features `agent.toml` names. |

## Run it

```sh
export DEEPGRAM_API_KEY=...  OPENAI_API_KEY=...  CARTESIA_API_KEY=...
export BRISVOX_AGENT_FILE=examples/rust-tools/agent.toml

# Validate the agent file first: offline, with line and column for every problem.
cargo run -p brisvox-example-rust-tools -- check "$BRISVOX_AGENT_FILE" --require-secrets

# Serve calls (websocket on 127.0.0.1:8080, health on :8081; see docs/OPERATIONS.md).
cargo run -p brisvox-example-rust-tools
```

The binary reads the same environment variables as the stock `brisvox-server`
(`docs/OPERATIONS.md`) and takes the same command line (`check`, `--help`, `--version`). Talk to
it with any client of the [websocket protocol](../../docs/WEBSOCKET_PROTOCOL.md), for example
`cargo run --release -p brisvox-bench -- v2v --url ws://127.0.0.1:8080/ --fixtures en_two_utterances --runs 1`,
and ask what time it is in Istanbul, or ask it to pass a message on.

## The two tools

| Tool | Kind | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `get_time(timezone)` | `ReadOnly` | Changes nothing, so the engine may start it before the caller has finished speaking (speculation) and cancels it on a barge-in. It reads the injected clock (`SharedClock::wall`), never the system clock. An argument it cannot use is a `ToolError` whose message tells the model what to try. |
| `save_note(text)` | `SideEffect` | Changes the world, so the engine never runs it speculatively and never twice for one call, and a barge-in does not cancel it. It still uses `ctx.idempotency_key().digest()` as the key of its effect, as a tool calling a real API must, so a redelivered request returns the same note (`already_saved: true`). |

Rules a tool follows (`docs/TOOLS.md`): no blocking or CPU-heavy work (move it to a blocking
pool), every IO await bounded by a timeout, state that outlives a call behind an `Arc` in your
`AppTools`, per-call data only from `ToolCallCtx`.

## Make it yours

1. Copy this directory next to your own code, or depend on `brisvox` from your own crate
   (next section).
2. Replace the tools in `src/lib.rs`. Each is a `Tool` (an async `call(args, ctx)`) plus a
   `ToolSpec` (name, description the model reads, JSON Schema of the arguments, `ToolKind`);
   arguments are validated against the schema before your code runs.
3. Name the tools in your agent file's `tools = [...]`. A name no tool provides is an error of
   `check` and of the server's start.
4. In `Cargo.toml`, enable the `brisvox` features your agent file needs: the `provider-*`
   of its three providers, plus `webrtc`, `smart-turn-ort` (for the `adaptive` turn policy),
   `call-control` or `otlp` as you use them. `all-providers` turns on every adapter.
5. Run `check` after every change to the agent file.

## Outside this repository

The brisvox crates are on crates.io. A standalone project is this `Cargo.toml` (to follow the
development branch instead, replace each `version` by `git = "https://github.com/bilal07karadeniz/brisvox"`
with a `rev` pinned to a commit you tested; a branch name moves under you):

```toml
[package]
name = "my-voice-agent"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"
rust-version = "1.99"

[dependencies]
# One dependency: the server, the Tool/ToolSpec types (`brisvox::agent::tools`) and the injected
# clock (`brisvox::core`) that src/lib.rs imports.
brisvox = { version = "0.1", features = [
    # The providers your agent file names (docs/CONFIG.md), or "all-providers".
    "provider-deepgram", "provider-openai", "provider-cartesia",
    # Optional, as in the README's "What to build with": "smart-turn-ort" (adaptive turns),
    # "webrtc" (browsers; needs cmake and a C compiler), "call-control" (telephony tools).
] }
serde_json = "1"
```

with `src/main.rs` and `src/lib.rs` copied from this directory. Three more things to copy or know:

* **The toolchain.** The crates use edition 2024 and need Rust 1.99 or newer (the repository's
  `rust-toolchain.toml` pins 1.99.0).
* **The lockfile.** Commit your own `Cargo.lock`. To start from the dependency versions the
  project was tested with, copy the repository's `Cargo.lock` next to your `Cargo.toml` once:
  cargo keeps those versions and drops the entries it does not use. A fresh resolution picks the
  newest compatible versions of every dependency instead.
* **A fully local agent** (no API key; sherpa-onnx speech recognition, an OpenAI-compatible LLM
  server such as Ollama, an OpenAI-compatible speech server such as Kokoro, see
  `book/src/quickstart/local.md`) takes these features:
  `provider-sherpa-onnx`, `provider-openai-compatible`, `provider-openai-speech`,
  `smart-turn-ort` and, for a browser, `webrtc`.

`get_time` accepts fixed UTC offsets only (`"UTC+3"`, `"+05:30"`), to keep the example free of a
time zone database; a real application would use `chrono-tz` or `jiff`.

## Tests

```sh
cargo nextest run -p brisvox-example-rust-tools
```

They register the tools, check their kinds, load `agent.toml` and resolve its tool names against
the registry (a renamed tool or a stale agent file fails here), and exercise both tools,
including the idempotency of `save_note`.


<!-- source: sdk/web/README.md -->

# @brisvox/web

The browser side of a Brisvox voice call, as **one dependency-free ES module**
(`brisvox-call.js`, with types in `brisvox-call.d.ts`). Put a "Talk to us" button on a website
without writing any audio code:

* **WebRTC first**: one WHIP request, Opus both ways, the browser's own echo cancellation, noise
  suppression and gain control on the microphone.
* **WebSocket fallback, by itself**: when WebRTC media cannot get through (a host with one HTTP
  port, a network that passes only HTTPS, a blocked UDP port), the module switches to the
  generic WebSocket audio protocol on the same port after 4 seconds
  (`docs/WEBSOCKET_PROTOCOL.md`). The microphone is resampled to 24 kHz PCM16 in an AudioWorklet
  and sent in 20 ms frames; the assistant's audio plays through a second worklet with an 80 ms
  jitter buffer (at most 400 ms, the oldest audio dropped beyond that). When the assistant is
  interrupted the server sends `clear` and the buffer is emptied at once, so the caller never
  hears the cut-off sentence finish.
* **One-port hosts: say so.** On a host that cannot receive UDP (a one-port platform such as Railway or Render, a plain
  HTTPS-only proxy) WebRTC never connects. Pass `transport: "websocket"` and the module goes
  straight to `/ws`: no 4 second wait for a WebRTC attempt that cannot succeed and no second
  session token. (`transport: "auto"`, the default, is for pages that must also work where UDP
  is open.)
* **Clean hang-up**: `hangup()` deletes the WHIP session, closes the sockets, stops the
  microphone tracks and closes the audio context. Closing the tab does the same.
* **Session tokens that work**: a token is single use, so the module asks your `tokenProvider`
  for a new one for every connection attempt (WebRTC, then the WebSocket).

The module is also what the server's built-in `/demo` page and `examples/web-assistant/web/index.html`
run, so those pages are a worked example of every option below.

Install from npm: `npm install @brisvox/web` (`npm i brisvox` re-exports it as `brisvox/web`). Or copy `brisvox-call.js` and `brisvox-call.d.ts` into
your project (they are two plain files), or depend on the folder from a checkout
(`"@brisvox/web": "file:../brisvox/sdk/web"`).

## Plain HTML

Serve `brisvox-call.js` next to your page. The server URL is the signaling port of
`brisvox-server` (`BRISVOX_WEBRTC_ADDR`: WebRTC at `/whip`, the WebSocket fallback at `/ws`), and
your backend hands out the token (see "Tokens" below).

```html
<button id="talk">Talk to us</button>
<span id="status"></span>

<script type="module">
  import { BrisvoxCall } from "/brisvox-call.js";

  const talk = document.getElementById("talk");
  const status = document.getElementById("status");
  let call = null;

  talk.addEventListener("click", async () => {
    if (call) { await call.hangup(); return; }     // second click: hang up

    call = new BrisvoxCall({
      serverUrl: "https://voice.example.com",
      // Called for every attempt: a session token is single use.
      tokenProvider: async () => {
        const res = await fetch("/api/voice-token", { method: "POST" });
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`token request failed (${res.status})`);
        return (await res.json()).token;
      },
      onEvent(event) {
        if (event.type === "state") {
          status.textContent = event.state === "connected" ? `Talking (${event.transport})` : event.state;
          if (event.state === "ended" || event.state === "failed") { call = null; talk.textContent = "Talk to us"; }
          if (event.state === "connected") talk.textContent = "Hang up";
        }
        if (event.type === "error") console.warn(event.message);
      },
    });
    try {
      await call.start();            // asks for the microphone, then connects
    } catch (error) {
      // already reported through onEvent ("error", then state "failed")
    }
  });
</script>
```

Call `start()` from a click handler: browsers only start audio after a user gesture, and the
module creates its audio context at that moment. The page must be on `https://` (or
`http://localhost`) for the microphone, and an `https://` page may only call an `https://` server.
If the page and the server have different origins, set `BRISVOX_WEBRTC_CORS_ORIGIN` on the server
to the page's origin (`docs/DEPLOY.md`).

## Next.js (App Router)

Two files: a route handler that mints a token for the visitor, and a client component with the
button. Put the module in your project, for example `app/lib/brisvox-call.js` and
`app/lib/brisvox-call.d.ts` (or `npm install @brisvox/web` and import it).

`app/api/voice-token/route.ts` (server side: the secret never reaches the browser):

```ts
import { createHmac, randomBytes } from "node:crypto";

// The same secret as BRISVOX_SESSION_SECRET on the Brisvox server (at least 32 bytes). A short
// secret can be guessed offline from one token, so refuse to start with one.
const SECRET = process.env.BRISVOX_SESSION_SECRET ?? "";
if (Buffer.byteLength(SECRET) < 32) {
  throw new Error("BRISVOX_SESSION_SECRET must be at least 32 bytes");
}

// The pages that may ask for a token: your own origin(s), exactly.
const ALLOWED_ORIGINS = new Set((process.env.VOICE_ALLOWED_ORIGINS ?? "https://www.example.com").split(","));

// A minimal per-IP limiter: 5 tokens a minute. It lives in this process's memory, so it is per
// server instance and starts over on a restart: enough to stop a loop in a browser tab, not a
// determined attacker. For a real limit use your platform's (Upstash, Redis, your CDN's rules).
const hits = new Map<string, number[]>();
function limited(ip: string, limit = 5, windowMs = 60_000): boolean {
  const now = Date.now();
  const recent = (hits.get(ip) ?? []).filter((t) => now - t < windowMs);
  if (recent.length >= limit) { hits.set(ip, recent); return true; }
  recent.push(now);
  hits.set(ip, recent);
  if (hits.size > 10_000) for (const [key, times] of hits) if (times.every((t) => now - t >= windowMs)) hits.delete(key);
  return false;
}

// A session token: `v1.<payload>.<signature>`, valid for one call, for a minute.
// (sdk/typescript exports the same thing as `mintSessionToken`.)
function mint(audience: string, ttlSeconds: number, claims: object = {}): string {
  const payload = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({
    aud: audience,
    exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + ttlSeconds,
    sid: randomBytes(16).toString("base64url"),
    ...claims,
  }));
  const signature = createHmac("sha256", SECRET).update(payload).digest();
  return `v1.${payload.toString("base64url")}.${signature.toString("base64url")}`;
}

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  // Every token you hand out is a call you pay for: put your own login check here too (the checks
  // below only keep other websites and loops away; a script can fake any header).
  // 1. Only your own pages: the browser always sends Origin on a cross-origin or POST request.
  const origin = request.headers.get("origin");
  if (!origin || !ALLOWED_ORIGINS.has(origin)) {
    return new Response("forbidden", { status: 403 });
  }
  // 2. Not too often from one address (behind a proxy, x-forwarded-for is the client's address
  //    only when YOUR proxy sets it; do not trust it on a server that is reachable directly).
  const ip = request.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0]?.trim() || "unknown";
  if (limited(ip)) {
    return new Response("too many calls", { status: 429, headers: { "Retry-After": "60" } });
  }
  const token = mint("brisvox-webrtc", 60, { max_s: 600 });
  return Response.json({ token }, { headers: { "Cache-Control": "no-store" } });
}
```

`app/components/TalkButton.tsx` (client side):

```tsx
"use client";

import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from "react";
import { BrisvoxCall, type CallEvent, type CallState } from "../lib/brisvox-call.js";

export default function TalkButton() {
  const callRef = useRef<BrisvoxCall | null>(null);
  const [state, setState] = useState<CallState>("idle");
  const [transport, setTransport] = useState<string | null>(null);
  const [message, setMessage] = useState("");

  // Leaving the page hangs up (the module also does it on `pagehide`).
  useEffect(() => () => { void callRef.current?.hangup(); }, []);

  async function toggle() {
    if (callRef.current) {
      await callRef.current.hangup();
      return;
    }
    const call = new BrisvoxCall({
      serverUrl: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_BRISVOX_URL!,           // https://voice.example.com
      tokenProvider: async () => {
        const res = await fetch("/api/voice-token", { method: "POST" });
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`token request failed (${res.status})`);
        return (await res.json()).token as string;
      },
      onEvent(event: CallEvent) {
        if (event.type === "state") {
          setState(event.state);
          setTransport(event.state === "connected" ? event.transport ?? null : null);
          if (event.state === "ended" || event.state === "failed") callRef.current = null;
        }
        if (event.type === "error") setMessage(event.message);
      },
    });
    callRef.current = call;
    setMessage("");
    try {
      await call.start();
    } catch {
      /* reported through onEvent */
    }
  }

  const busy = state === "connecting";
  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={toggle} disabled={busy}>
        {state === "connected" ? "Hang up" : busy ? "Connecting..." : "Talk to us"}
      </button>
      {state === "connected" && <span> Talking ({transport})</span>}
      {message && <p role="alert">{message}</p>}
    </div>
  );
}
```

Use it from any page: `import TalkButton from "./components/TalkButton"` and render `<TalkButton />`.
The module only touches browser APIs inside `start()`, so importing it during server rendering is
harmless, but keep the component a client component (`"use client"`).

## Options

| Option | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `serverUrl` | required | The server's `http(s)://` address (the signaling port). |
| `token` / `tokenProvider` | none | A fixed bearer token, or an async function returning one. The provider is called for every attempt. Not both. |
| `transport` | `"auto"` | `"auto"`: WebRTC, then the WebSocket. `"webrtc"`: never fall back. `"websocket"`: skip WebRTC. |
| `fallbackAfterMs` | `4000` | How long WebRTC gets to connect, from the moment the server accepted its offer, before the WebSocket takes over. A failed connection falls back at once. |
| `signalingTimeoutMs` | `10000` | Bound on the WHIP request (a timeout counts as "no way to reach the server": fall back). |
| `connectTimeoutMs` | `20000` | With `transport: "webrtc"`: how long the connection may take. |
| `startTimeoutMs` | `8000` | WebSocket: from connecting to the server's `started`. |
| `whipPath` / `wsPath` | `/whip`, `/ws` | Paths on `serverUrl`. `null` turns that transport off. |
| `audio` | echo cancellation, noise suppression, auto gain, mono | Merged over the microphone constraints, for example `{ deviceId }`. |
| `audioElement` | a new `Audio()` | The element that plays the assistant over WebRTC. |
| `workletUrl` | a Blob URL | Load the AudioWorklet from a URL instead (a strict Content-Security-Policy that forbids `blob:` needs this; the file's content is the exported `WORKLET_SOURCE`). |
| `metadata` | `{}` | Extra string pairs sent in the WebSocket `start` message. |
| `onEvent` | none | Receives every event; `call.subscribe(fn)` adds more listeners. |

`await call.start()` resolves when the call is connected and rejects with a `BrisvoxCallError`
(`error.code` is `config`, `unsupported`, `microphone`, `token`, `signaling`, `webrtc`,
`websocket`, `timeout` or `connection`; `error.status` is the HTTP status when the server
answered one). `connect(options)` is `new BrisvoxCall(options)` plus `start()`.

Other members: `call.state`, `call.transport`, `await call.hangup()`, `call.setMuted(true)`,
`call.getLevels()` (`{ mic, bot }`, each 0 to 1, for a level meter), `call.audioContext`.

## Events

| `event.type` | Fields | When |
|---|---|---|
| `state` | `state` (`connecting`, `connected`, `ended`, `failed`), `previous`, `transport`, `reason`, `error` | Every state change. `connected` carries the transport; `ended` and `failed` carry the reason. Media that drops for a moment shows as `connecting` and then `connected` again. |
| `transport` | `transport` (`webrtc` or `websocket`), `fallback`, `reason` | A transport carries the call. `fallback` is true when WebRTC was tried first. |
| `fallback` | `from`, `to`, `reason` | WebRTC could not connect and the WebSocket is next. |
| `started` | `callId`, `sampleRate`, `encoding` | WebSocket: the server opened the call. |
| `clear` | `epoch` | Barge-in on the WebSocket: the unplayed audio was dropped. (Over WebRTC the server stops sending.) |
| `mark` | `id` | WebSocket: a playback mark; the module echoes it once the audio before it has played. |
| `stop` | `reason` | The server ended the call. |
| `notice` | `code`, `message`, `fatal` | A server `error` message (`docs/WEBSOCKET_PROTOCOL.md`). |
| `message` | `message` | A server message of a type this version does not know. The protocols carry no transcripts today; if a server sends them, they arrive here unchanged. |
| `muted` | `muted` | `setMuted` was called. |
| `error` | `error`, `code`, `message`, `fatal` | The call failed; `state` `failed` follows. |
| `log` | `text` | A line for a connection log. |

## Tokens

A server that listens beyond localhost requires credentials (`docs/SECURITY.md`). For a real site
set `BRISVOX_SESSION_SECRET` on the server and mint a **session token** on your backend for each
visitor (audience `brisvox-webrtc` for the signaling listener, which also serves `/ws`). The
token is short-lived (30 to 120 seconds are enough: it is only needed until the call starts) and
**single use**, which is why `tokenProvider` is called again for the WebSocket fallback instead of
reusing the first token. The module sends it as `Authorization: Bearer` for WebRTC and as the
`brisvox-token.<token>` WebSocket subprotocol (or `?token=` when it has characters a subprotocol
cannot carry). Never put the secret, or a long-lived token, in the page. `token` (a fixed string)
is for development against `BRISVOX_WEBRTC_TOKEN`.

## Behaviour worth knowing

* A refused request is shown, not hidden by a second transport: a `401`/`403` or `503` from the
  signaling endpoint fails the call with `code: "signaling"` and `status`. Only "no WebRTC here",
  "the request could not be made" and "media did not connect" fall back.
* Hanging up while the call is still opening cancels it: `start()` rejects with an error named
  `AbortError` and nothing stays open.
* Over WebSocket the module bounds what it buffers: microphone frames are dropped while the socket
  is more than 128 KiB behind, bot audio is dropped while the playback worklet lags by more than
  96 KiB.
* A browser without `AudioWorklet` (or a page that is not a secure context) can still use WebRTC;
  the fallback then reports `code: "unsupported"`.
* The module opens one `AudioContext` per call and closes it in `hangup()`; make one
  `BrisvoxCall` per call.

## Tests

```sh
cd sdk/web && node scripts/run-tests.mjs        # Node 20.4+, no install step
```

The tests (`test/`) drive the module with fake `WebSocket`, `RTCPeerConnection`, `AudioContext`,
`AudioWorkletNode`, `getUserMedia` and `fetch` objects (passed through the `platform` option):
WebRTC success, WebRTC timeout and the WebSocket fallback with a fresh token, forcing a
transport, hang-up cleanup, barge-in `clear`, marks, back-pressure, error events. `worklet.test.mjs`
runs the AudioWorklet code (resampling, 20 ms framing, jitter buffer, marks, clear) against fake
audio. The tests run on node's mock timers (`ftest`, `drive`, `until` in `test/fakes.mjs`; Node
20.4+), so they never wait for real time. `scripts/verify.sh` runs them next to the TypeScript
SDK's, and then compiles `test/types-check.ts` (a usage sample) with `tsc --noEmit --strict` using
the compiler the TypeScript SDK stage installed; without that compiler the check is skipped with a
warning.


<!-- source: docs/WEBSOCKET_PROTOCOL.md -->

# Brisvox websocket protocol, version 1

Status: version 1. Code: `brisvox_transport::websocket` (`protocol.rs` is the executable
definition, `connection.rs` the server side, `client.rs` the reference client). Design and
bounds: `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, "WebSocket transport".

One websocket connection is one call. **Binary frames carry audio, text frames carry one JSON
object each** with a `type` field. The server speaks plain `ws://`; terminate TLS (`wss://`) in
front of it (a reverse proxy). The server does not look at the request path. The protocol has
no authentication of its own, but the upgrade request can be checked (
`docs/SECURITY.md`): with `BRISVOX_SESSION_SECRET` the client must present a session token your
backend minted (`aud` `brisvox-ws`, short-lived, single use), with `BRISVOX_WS_TOKEN` a static
one (development). The token travels in `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, in the WebSocket
subprotocol `brisvox-token.<token>` (a browser: `new WebSocket(url, ["brisvox",
"brisvox-token." + token])`; the server selects `brisvox`), or in `?token=<token>`. A missing
token is HTTP 401, an invalid, expired, reused or wrong-audience one 403, an oversize one (over
4 KiB) 413; every answer carries `Cache-Control: no-store`. The token's `sid`, `agent`, `max_s`
and `meta` reach the call's metadata as `session_id`, `session.agent`, `session.max_s` and
`session.meta.<key>` (the client's own `start.metadata` cannot set those keys; `max_s` is
reported, not enforced, on this listener). The server binary keeps this listener on loopback,
or off next to another listener, unless `BRISVOX_WS_ADDR` says otherwise, and **refuses a
non-loopback `BRISVOX_WS_ADDR` without `BRISVOX_SESSION_SECRET` or `BRISVOX_WS_TOKEN`** unless
`BRISVOX_INSECURE_LISTENERS=1` (`docs/OPERATIONS.md`).

**Also on the WebRTC signaling port.** With `brisvox-server --features webrtc`, the
signaling listener (`BRISVOX_WEBRTC_ADDR`) serves this same protocol on a WebSocket upgrade at
`BRISVOX_WEBRTC_WS_PATH` (default `/ws`), so a browser whose network cannot carry WebRTC media can
still call over the one HTTP(S) port. The connection and call code is this transport's; what differs is
the listener around it. The upgrade is judged like `POST /whip`: the signaling listener's token
(static `BRISVOX_WEBRTC_TOKEN` or a session token with `aud` `brisvox-webrtc`, in the same three
places as above), its `Origin` rule, its offer rate, per-address call cap and handshake pool, and
the call limit (HTTP 401, 403, 413, 429, 503 before the upgrade), and a session token's `max_s`
**is** enforced here (the call ends with `stop{ended}`), unlike on the standalone `BRISVOX_WS_ADDR` listener above, which only reports it. The call's metadata is as above with
`transport` `webrtc-ws` (the server's logs and metrics label the call the same way). The browser module `sdk/web/brisvox-call.js` (and with it the bundled
pages `/demo` and `examples/web-assistant/web/index.html`)
use it as their fallback with 24 kHz `pcm16`, 20 ms frames, an 80 ms playback buffer, and echo
`mark` once the audio before it has played.

## Audio
- Mono, in both directions, at the `sample_rate` and `encoding` the client gave in `start`:
  - `pcm16`: 16-bit signed little-endian samples. A frame must be whole samples (even length).
  - `mulaw`: G.711 mu-law, one byte per sample (telephony; typically 8000 Hz).
- Sample rates: 8000, 16000, 22050, 24000, 44100 or 48000 Hz.
- A frame may hold any amount of audio up to `max_audio_bytes` (default 64 KiB). Send 20 ms
  frames: that is the unit the engine paces and clears at. An empty binary frame is ignored.
- The server sends bot audio at real time (one 20 ms frame per 20 ms), already in the call's
  rate and encoding. The transport itself does not resample: audio at another rate than the
  call's is dropped, with one `output_rate_mismatch` notice per call. The engine never sends
  such audio: it reads the call's rate from the transport's `Started` event and its TTS stage
  resamples the provider's audio (24 kHz by default) to it in exact 20 ms frames, so any client
  rate works with any provider rate (an 8 kHz mu-law call with a 24 kHz TTS: 160-byte frames,
  about 7 us per frame in release; `crates/brisvox-engine/tests/ws_mulaw_call.rs`).
- Allocation: pcm16 frames pass without a copy in both directions; the mu-law conversion writes
  into a per-connection buffer allocated in 16 KiB chunks. A chunk serves 51 decoded frames (320
  bytes: 20 ms at 8 kHz) or 102 encoded frames (160 bytes), so about one allocation per 50
  frames from the client and one per 100 frames to it (unit-tested in `connection.rs`).

## Client to server

| `type` | fields | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `start` | `version` (1), `sample_rate`, `encoding` (`pcm16` default, or `mulaw`), `call_id` (optional, at most 128 bytes), `metadata` (optional string map, at most 32 entries, keys up to 64 bytes, values up to 256 bytes) | Opens the call. Must be the first message. A client should send nothing else before it has `started`; the server does not enforce that: audio, `dtmf` and `mark` that arrive between `start` and `started` are accepted and passed on. The rate keys of the call's metadata belong to the server: a client-supplied `sample_rate` is overwritten and `input_sample_rate` / `output_sample_rate` are removed (the call has one symmetric rate). |
| `dtmf` | `digit`: one of `0-9 * # A-D` (`a-d` are accepted too and mean the same) | A key press. |
| `mark` | `id` (at most 256 bytes) | Echo of a server `mark`: everything the server sent before it has been played. |
| `stop` | | The client hangs up. |

Unknown fields are ignored. A text frame larger than `max_control_bytes` (default 16 KiB) is an
error.

## Server to client

| `type` | fields | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `started` | `version`, `call_id`, `sample_rate`, `encoding` | The call is open. Bot audio can follow from here. |
| `clear` | `epoch` | Barge-in. Drop everything not yet played, including audio and marks buffered on the client; audio sent after this message belongs to the new epoch. Marks that were cut are never echoed (an echo of one is ignored anyway). |
| `mark` | `id` (at most 256 bytes) | Echo this id as a `mark` once all audio sent before it has played. The server does not send a mark with a longer id (non-fatal `mark_id_too_long` instead; the engine gets no `MarkPlayed` for it), because the client's echo of it would be refused. |
| `stop` | `reason`: `ended` (the engine hung up, or the client's own `stop` was processed) or `shutdown` (the server stops) | The call is over; the server closes the connection next. |
| `error` | `code`, `message`, `fatal` | A protocol fault. A fatal error is followed by a close frame; a non-fatal one is informational. |

`message` is for humans and never contains credentials or audio.

## Lifecycle
1. The client connects (HTTP upgrade). If the server is at `max_calls` (or, in
   `brisvox-server`, at `BRISVOX_MAX_SESSIONS`), the answer is HTTP 503 with `Retry-After: 1`,
   and no websocket exists. A `brisvox-server` whose inference pool is overloaded (`5`) or whose
   provider budget is exhausted (`2`) answers 503 with a longer `Retry-After` the same way. A
   `brisvox-server` that is draining for a shutdown answers HTTP 503
   without `Retry-After`: connect to another instance (`docs/OPERATIONS.md`).
2. The client sends `start` within `start_timeout` (default 5 s).
3. The server validates it and answers `started` (or a fatal `error`, then a close).
4. Audio and control flow both ways. The server pings every `ping_interval` (default 10 s); a
   standard client answers pongs automatically. Any frame from the client counts as life. No frame
   for `ping_timeout` (default 30 s) ends the call with `ping_timeout`.
5. The call ends when:
   - the client sends `stop`: the server answers `stop{ended}` and closes (engine: `PeerHangup`);
   - the client sends a close frame (engine: `PeerHangup`). The server answers with a close frame
     (RFC 6455 5.5.1), but it cannot send `stop` after it read the client's close frame, so a client
     that wants the `stop` message should send `stop` and wait for the server's close. `stop`
     followed at once by a close frame (a browser's `send(stop); close()`) works: the server holds
     back reading the close frame until it has sent `stop{ended}`, and the engine sees
     `PeerHangup`;
   - the engine hangs up: `stop{ended}`, close 1000;
   - the server shuts down: `stop{shutdown}`, close 1001;
   - the connection breaks without a close frame, an EOF or a reset (engine: `PeerDisconnected`,
     and no `error` event: a vanished peer is not a protocol violation, there is nobody to report
     it to);
   - a fatal error, a ping timeout or a stuck client (below).

## Errors and close codes
The close codes below are asserted by `tests/websocket.rs` (a client branches on them: 1013 means
retry later); 1000 is the engine's hang-up and 1001 the server's shutdown.

| `code` | fatal | close code | when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `invalid_json` | yes | 1002 | a text frame that is not a JSON object with a string `type` |
| `invalid_message` | yes | 1002 / 1008 | a known `type` with missing or invalid fields (bad digit, bad `start`, too long id, `start` not first) |
| `unknown_message` | no (yes before `start`) | | an unknown `type`; ignored once the call is open. More than 16 faults on one call end it with `too_many_errors` |
| `unsupported_version` | yes | 1008 | `start.version` is not 1 |
| `unsupported_sample_rate` | yes | 1008 | `start.sample_rate` is not a supported rate |
| `unexpected_start` | yes | 1008 | a second `start` |
| `audio_before_start` | yes | 1008 | a binary frame before `start` |
| `start_timeout` | yes | 1008 | no `start` in time |
| `bad_audio` | yes | 1008 | a pcm16 frame with an odd byte count |
| `frame_too_large` | yes | 1009 | a binary or text frame over its limit (or over the websocket layer's limit; that error may be lost to a connection reset) |
| `too_many_errors` | yes | 1008 | see `unknown_message` |
| `output_rate_mismatch` | no | | the engine produced audio at another rate than the call's; dropped, reported once per call |
| `mark_id_too_long` | no | | the engine asked for a mark with an id over 256 bytes; the mark is not sent |
| `server_busy` | yes | 1013 | the engine is not taking new calls |
| `overloaded` | yes | 1013 | the engine takes no input from the call for `send_timeout` |
| `ping_timeout` | yes | 1008 | see Lifecycle |

A client that does not take bot audio (its socket stays full for `write_timeout`, default 5 s) is
disconnected without a message, since nothing more can be written to it. Playout is real time, so
the server never buffers more than a few frames for a slow client. When the engine hangs up or the
server shuts down while the client is stuck, the blocked write is abandoned at once and the
goodbye gets at most `min(write_timeout, close_grace)`.

## Server configuration
`ServerConfig::validate` (called when the server starts) refuses: `ping_timeout` not longer than
`ping_interval`, `ping_interval` under 10 ms, a zero timeout or `close_grace`, `max_calls` or
`accept_queue` of 0, `max_audio_bytes` under 2, `max_control_bytes` under 512. The websocket layer
itself accepts frames up to the larger of `max_audio_bytes` and `max_control_bytes` (a frame above
that is refused as `frame_too_large` by the layer, with a close that may reach the client as a
reset when much of the frame is unread); the smaller limit is enforced by the connection.

## Marks and barge-in, from the client's side
A phone-like client keeps a playout buffer. It plays binary frames in order. When it receives
`mark`, it remembers the id and sends `mark{id}` back when the audio received before the mark has
finished playing. On `clear` it empties the buffer at once and forgets pending marks. This is what
the reference client does, and what makes `MarkPlayed` mean "the caller heard it" and what lets the
engine trim its LLM context to what was actually spoken.

## Reference client
`cargo run -p brisvox-transport --bin ws_client -- <URL> <INPUT.wav> <OUTPUT.wav> [options]`

Streams a mono 16-bit WAV (for instance `fixtures/en_two_utterances.wav`, 16 kHz) as real-time
20 ms frames, answers marks, and writes the bot audio it received to `OUTPUT.wav` (the
concatenation of what played; a `clear` removes the audio that had not played yet). After the
input ends it waits until the server has been silent for `--linger-ms` (default 2000)
(pending marks are echoed first, even if that takes longer), sends `stop` and waits for the server
to close.

Options: `--encoding pcm16|mulaw`, `--no-realtime` (send as fast as the server takes it; the
client keeps reading its socket between and during the sends, so a server that is already
producing audio is not stalled by it),
`--linger-ms N`, `--dtmf KEYS` (pressed right after `started`), `--meta KEY=VALUE` (repeatable).
Exit codes: 0 success, 1 the call failed, 2 bad usage or an unreadable or unwritable file. The call
failed (`ClientReport::failure`) when the server reported a fatal error, the connection broke
(a read or write error, or the stream ended without a close frame) before the server stopped the
call, the server closed the connection without `stop` before all input was sent, or
`max_duration` passed. The recording is written in every case, and the error is printed. A server
`stop` while input was still being sent (the bot hung up) is not a failure.

## Compatibility
The version is the integer in `start.version`/`started.version`. A change that an old peer cannot
ignore (a new required field, a changed meaning) bumps it. Adding message types and fields does
not: peers ignore unknown fields, and an unknown `type` is non-fatal.


<!-- source: docs/RTVI.md -->

# RTVI: connecting a Pipecat client to brisvox

`brisvox_transport::rtvi` (feature `rtvi`, on by default) lets the Pipecat client SDKs talk to a
brisvox server: `@pipecat-ai/client-js` with `@pipecat-ai/websocket-transport`. Protocol facts,
sources and the list of unverified points are in `docs/providers/rtvi.md` (RTVI 2.1.0, fetched and
fact-checked 2026-10-08). The module documentation (`crates/brisvox-transport/src/rtvi/mod.rs`)
is the reference for behavior; this page is how to use it and how to check it by hand.

> **Not the same listener.** The WebSocket fallback of the WebRTC signaling port
> (`docs/DEPLOY.md`) carries the generic protocol of `docs/WEBSOCKET_PROTOCOL.md`, not RTVI. A
> Pipecat client SDK keeps using `BRISVOX_RTVI_ADDR`, which is already one HTTP(S) port and works
> on one-port hosts (such as Railway) without further steps.

## Server side

```rust
let mut server = RtviServer::bind(ServerConfig::default(), RtviConfig::default(),
                                  SystemClock::shared(), &cancel).await?;
while let Some(call) = server.accept_call(&cancel).await? {
    // call.link   -> TransportSession::open(clock, call.link, SessionConfig::default(), &cancel)
    // call.sender -> RtviSender: send(RtviEvent::..), respond(id, t, d), respond_error(id, msg)
    // call.inbox  -> RtviInbox: client-message / send-text / llm-function-call-result requests
}
```

- One WebSocket path (`RtviConfig::path`, default `/rtvi`); the client accepts any path.
- Audio: 16 kHz in (the JS client's `recorderSampleRate` default), 24 kHz out (its
  `playerSampleRate` default). The JS client ignores the `sample_rate` of bot audio and plays at its
  own rate, so `RtviConfig::output_rate` must equal the client's `playerSampleRate`. The engine reads
  both rates from `CallInfo::sample_rate()` (`input_sample_rate` / `output_sample_rate` metadata).
- `Transport::accept` also works and gives only the `CallLink` (no RTVI events, client requests are
  answered with errors).
- Terminate TLS in front of the listener (`wss://`). The protocol has no authentication of its
  own; the upgrade checks are `RtviConfig::sessions` (short-lived single-use session tokens,
  `BRISVOX_SESSION_SECRET`, the production way), `RtviConfig::token` (a shared static token,
  development) and `allowed_origins`. The server binary refuses to bind a non-loopback RTVI
  address with neither a session secret nor a token (`BRISVOX_INSECURE_LISTENERS=1` overrides;
  `docs/SECURITY.md`).
- The token travels in `?token=` (what the Pipecat client SDKs append; it lands in proxy logs and
  browser history), in `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, or in the WebSocket subprotocol
  `brisvox-token.<token>`: a browser page offers `["brisvox", "brisvox-token." + token]` and the
  server selects `brisvox`. A missing token is HTTP 401, an invalid, expired, reused or
  wrong-audience one 403, an oversize one (over 4 KiB) 413. Every refusal and the accepted
  upgrade carry `Cache-Control: no-store`. A session token's claims reach the call's metadata
  (`session_id`, `session.agent`, `session.meta.<key>`); `max_s` is reported, not enforced, here.

### With the engine

`brisvox_engine::rtvi::RtviBridge` connects a call's `RtviSender` and `RtviInbox` to the engine:

```rust
let config = RtviConfig::default(); // the bridge switches the adapter's speaking events off per call
// ... accept_call as above, then for each call:
let (builder, bridge) = RtviBridge::attach(builder, call.sender, call.inbox,
                                           RtviBridgeConfig::default(), Some(handler), clock.clone(), &cancel);
let session = TransportSession::open(clock, call.link, SessionConfig::default(), &cancel).await?;
let call = run_call(session, builder, &cancel).await?; // keep `bridge` alive as long as the call
```

- The client gets `user-started/stopped-speaking` (the user's turn), `user-transcription`,
  `user-llm-text`, `bot-llm-started/text/stopped`, `bot-tts-started/text/stopped`, `bot-output`,
  `bot-started/stopped-speaking` (the transport's playout), `bot-interrupted`, `metrics` (one per
  turn) and `error`, all on one queue. The mapping table is in the module docs
  (`crates/brisvox-engine/src/rtvi.rs`); the events come from `brisvox_engine::events`. Every
  `user-started-speaking` gets its `user-stopped-speaking`, also for a turn that ends without
  words (noise, an empty STT final), a turn superseded while its end waited for a final, and the
  hang-up.
- `send-text` becomes a user turn (`brisvox_engine::text_input`): it interrupts the bot if it is
  thinking or speaking, the runner appends the text to the context as a user message and answers
